name: Japanese Highball
description: Whisky and soda, built with a precision bordering on ceremony: frozen glass, hard ice, thirteen stirs. Japan turned the simplest drink into a discipline.
funFact: Suntory's 1950s highball campaign was a deliberate rescue of a collapsing whisky market, and it worked so completely that the highball is now the default way Japan drinks whisky.

steps: Freeze the glass and fill it to the top with hard, clear ice.
Pour the whisky over the ice and stir exactly thirteen times to chill it without melting the ice.
Add more ice if the level has dropped, then pour the chilled soda down the side in one steady motion.
Stir once, vertically, lifting the bar spoon straight out to keep the carbonation.
Express a lemon peel over the surface and serve immediately.

name: Mizuwari
description: Whisky and still water, one to two and a half, stirred over ice. The most-drunk whisky serve in Japan and the hardest to make well.
funFact: Japan's soft, low-mineral water is part of the point — mizuwari made with hard water tastes noticeably different, which is why the ratio travels badly.

steps: Fill a tall glass to the top with hard ice and let it chill the glass.
Pour in the whisky and stir thirteen and a half times, in the traditional count.
Top up the ice, then add the still water.
Stir three and a half times only — any more and the drink goes flat and watery.
Serve with food rather than on its own.

name: Oyuwari
description: Shochu cut with hot water, poured water-first so the two mix by convection alone. Kyushu's winter default.
funFact: The order is not superstition: pouring hot water first and shochu second lets the density difference mix the drink without stirring, which keeps the aroma intact.

steps: Warm a ceramic cup with a little hot water and discard it.
Pour the hot water into the cup FIRST, filling it about three-fifths.
Add the shochu on top and do not stir — the convection mixes it.
Rest for thirty seconds so the temperature settles to about 45°C.
Drink while hot, alongside food.
recipe.garnish: A slice of pickled plum, optional

name: Chuhai
description: Shochu and carbonated water with a fruit flavour — sold canned in a hundred varieties and poured fresh in every izakaya.
funFact: The name shortens 'shochu highball'. Canned chuhai is a vast category in Japan, with strong versions at 9% sold in the same fridge as the 3% ones and colour-coded accordingly.

ingredients.item: Fresh fruit or syrup (peach, grape, ume)

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu and the fruit syrup or muddled fresh fruit.
Top with well-chilled soda water.
Stir once, vertically, to preserve the fizz.
Garnish with a slice of the fruit used.
recipe.garnish: A slice of the matching fruit

name: Denki Bran
description: 'Electric Brandy' — a brandy, gin, wine and herb blend served at the same Tokyo bar since 1882, when electricity itself was the novelty.
funFact: Kamiya Bar in Asakusa has served it since 1882 and named it for electricity because anything modern and slightly shocking was 'denki' at the time; the recipe is still secret.

steps: Pour the Denki Bran into a small tumbler — no ice, no dilution.
Serve a small glass of cold draught beer alongside.
Sip the Denki Bran, then chase with the beer.
Do not mix the two; the pairing is the tradition.

name: Hoppy
description: Shochu topped with Hoppy, a near beer-flavoured mixer from 1948. Order 'naka' for more shochu and 'soto' for more Hoppy.
funFact: Hoppy was launched in 1948 when real beer was unaffordable, as a way to make cheap shochu taste like beer; postwar nostalgia has kept it on Tokyo izakaya menus ever since.

steps: Chill the mug and the Hoppy thoroughly; keep the shochu in the freezer.
Pour the frozen shochu into the mug — this is the 'naka'.
Add the cold Hoppy in one pour from a height to build a head.
Do not stir; the pour mixes it.
Order another 'naka' when the shochu runs out before the Hoppy does.

name: Yuzu Sour
description: Shochu or vodka with yuzu juice and soda — sharper and more floral than lemon, and unmistakably Japanese.
funFact: Yuzu is too sour and too seedy to eat, so it is grown almost entirely for its juice and peel — a citrus cultivated purely as a flavouring.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu, yuzu juice and honey syrup and stir to combine.
Top with chilled soda water.
Stir once vertically.
Garnish with a strip of yuzu peel.

name: Calpis Sour
description: Shochu with Calpis, the cloudy fermented-milk cordial that has been Japan's comfort drink since 1919. Tastes like a yoghurt lemonade.
funFact: Calpis was created in 1919 by a Japanese businessman who had encountered fermented mare's milk in Inner Mongolia; the name blends 'calcium' with the Sanskrit 'sarpis'.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu and Calpis concentrate and stir until fully combined.
Top with chilled soda water.
Stir once, gently — Calpis foams easily.
Serve with no garnish.

name: Sakerinha
description: A Caipirinha built on sake — the drink of Brazil's Japanese community, and of Japan's Brazilian one.
funFact: Brazil has the largest Japanese population outside Japan, and hundreds of thousands of Brazilian-Japanese later moved back to Japan — the drink travelled in both directions with them.

steps: Muddle the lime wedges with the sugar in a sturdy rocks glass.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour over the sake.
Stir hard from the bottom up until the glass frosts.
Serve with the spent lime still in the glass.

name: Baijiu Sour
description: Baijiu shaken with citrus, honey and egg white — Shanghai's project to make the world's best-selling spirit approachable to outsiders.
funFact: Baijiu outsells whisky, vodka and rum combined by volume, yet almost none of it leaves China — Shanghai's bar scene spent the 2010s working out how to mix it for people who did not grow up with it.

steps: Dry-shake the baijiu, lemon juice, honey syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters across the foam and draw a pattern through them.
Serve immediately.

name: Cynar Spritz
description: The spritz for people who find Aperol too sweet: artichoke amaro, prosecco and soda, darker and considerably more bitter.
funFact: Cynar is made from thirteen botanicals including artichoke leaves, and in the Veneto it is drunk as a spritz far more often than it is drunk neat.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the Cynar, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once, gently, to combine without killing the bubbles.
Garnish with an orange slice and an olive if you are in the Veneto.

name: Select Spritz
description: Venice's own spritz, made with Select rather than Aperol — deeper red, more bitter, and the local order since 1920.
funFact: Select was created in Venice in 1920 and remains the city's default spritz base; ordering an Aperol spritz in a Venetian bacaro marks you out immediately as being from elsewhere.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the Select and then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a green olive — not an orange slice, which is the Padova style.

name: Puccini
description: Prosecco over fresh mandarin juice — the winter member of Harry's Bar's painter-and-composer family.
funFact: Harry's Bar named its sparkling drinks after Venetian artists and composers, and made each with whatever fruit was in season — the Puccini belongs to mandarin season in midwinter.

steps: Squeeze fresh mandarins and strain the juice; chill it thoroughly.
Pour the cold juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco, stirring gently with a bar spoon as you pour.
Serve immediately, with no garnish.

name: Tintoretto
description: Pomegranate and prosecco — the deepest red of the Harry's Bar family, named for the painter who filled the Scuola di San Rocco.
funFact: Tintoretto spent over twenty years decorating the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, often working for nothing to keep rivals out — a level of commitment the drink does not attempt to match.

steps: Juice fresh pomegranate and strain out the solids.
Chill the juice thoroughly before use.
Pour the juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco and stir once with a bar spoon.
Garnish with a few pomegranate seeds.

name: Carajillo 43
description: Licor 43 shaken over espresso until it foams — Mexico's after-dinner drink, and ordered in vast quantities across the country.
funFact: Spain's carajillo is coffee with brandy or rum; Mexico rebuilt it around Licor 43 and shakes it cold, which is now so dominant that the Spanish original is barely known there.

ingredients.amount: cubed, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Pull a fresh espresso and let it cool for a few seconds.
Add the Licor 43 and espresso to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds until a thick crema forms.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Serve immediately, while the foam holds.

name: Mastiha Spritz
description: Chios mastiha with soda and citrus — resinous, pine-fresh and made from the tears of a tree that grows nowhere else on earth.
funFact: Mastic resin is harvested only in southern Chios — attempts to grow the trees productively elsewhere have consistently failed — and the villages that farm it are collectively called the Mastichochoria.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the mastiha and the lemon juice.
Pour in the prosecco, then top with soda water.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a lemon twist and a sprig of thyme.

name: Herrengedeck
description: A beer with a glass of sparkling wine beside it — 'the gentlemen's set menu', and a genuine Berlin tradition rather than a joke.
glassware: Beer glass and a sekt flute
funFact: In the West it means beer and sekt; in the former East it usually meant beer and a shot of clear spirit, and Berliners will still tell you which version their side of the city drank.

steps: Pour the pilsner into a beer glass and let the head settle.
Pour the chilled sekt into a separate small flute.
Serve the two side by side, not mixed.
Alternate between them — the sekt resets the palate between mouthfuls of beer.

name: Cubanito
description: Havana's Bloody Mary: rum instead of vodka, with lime, Worcestershire and a heavy hand of hot sauce.
funFact: Cuba's answer to the Bloody Mary predates most of the vodka versions, for the simple reason that Havana had excellent rum and almost no vodka.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, Worcestershire and hot sauce.
Top with tomato juice and season with salt and pepper.
Roll the drink between two tins rather than shaking, to mix without frothing.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Grzaniec
description: Mulled beer or wine with honey, cloves and ginger — Polish winter, served in mountain shelters and Christmas markets alike.
funFact: The beer version — grzane piwo — is the older of the two, and mulling beer was standard across northern Europe long before mulled wine became the Christmas default.

steps: Warm the beer or wine gently with the spices and orange peel — never boil it.
Hold at about 70°C for ten minutes so the spices infuse.
Stir in the honey until fully dissolved.
Strain into a heatproof mug.
Serve hot with a cinnamon stick.

name: Almdudler Spritzer
description: White wine with Almdudler, the Alpine herb soda that Austria treats as a national institution.
funFact: Almdudler has been made since 1957 from 32 Alpine herbs and is so entrenched that Austrians describe it as the country's second national drink after beer.

steps: Chill both the wine and the Almdudler well.
Pour the wine into a tall glass.
Top with the Almdudler.
Stir once, gently, and serve without ice in the Austrian manner.

name: Dutch Mule
description: Jenever with ginger beer and lime — the mule format handed to the malty grandfather of gin, which changes it entirely.
funFact: Jenever is distilled from malt wine and tastes closer to a light whisky than to London dry gin, which is why it holds up against ginger where gin can disappear.

steps: Fill a copper mug or highball with ice.
Add the jenever and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Irish Mule
description: Irish whiskey with ginger beer and lime. The mule's gentlest branch, and the one that goes down fastest.
funFact: Irish whiskey's triple distillation leaves it lighter and smoother than Scotch or bourbon, which is exactly why it disappears into ginger beer so easily.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the Irish whiskey and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge and a mint sprig.

name: Sima
description: Finnish spring mead: lemon, sugar and yeast fermented for a couple of days and bottled with raisins that float when it is ready.
funFact: The raisins are a timer: a few are dropped into each bottle, and when they rise to the surface the fermentation has produced enough carbonation to drink.

steps: Boil the water with both sugars and the lemon slices, then cool to lukewarm.
Stir in the yeast and leave covered at room temperature overnight.
Bottle, adding a teaspoon of sugar and a few raisins to each bottle.
Leave at room temperature until the raisins float, usually two to three days.
Refrigerate and drink within a week, at Vappu if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: The floating raisins and a lemon slice

name: Medovukha
description: Honey fermented with water and spices — an East Slavic drink older than distillation, lighter and quicker than true mead.
funFact: Traditional medovukha was fermented for decades; the boiled quick version was developed in the fifteenth century because nobody wanted to wait twenty years for a drink.

steps: Boil the water and honey together, skimming the foam that rises.
Add the spices and hops, simmer briefly, then cool to lukewarm.
Pitch the yeast and ferment in a covered vessel for about a week.
Strain and bottle, then refrigerate for several days to carbonate lightly.
Serve cool in ceramic mugs.

name: Uvita
description: Sweet red wine with grape must and spices, warmed and drunk at winter festivals along the Uruguayan coast.
funFact: Uruguay drinks more wine per head than any other country in the Americas, most of it Tannat, and its winter street festivals run on warmed sweet wine rather than beer.

steps: Combine the wine, must, sugar and spices in a pan.
Warm gently to about 65°C without boiling.
Hold for fifteen minutes so the spices infuse.
Strain into small glasses.
Serve warm, with the orange peel.

name: Íslenskur Kaffi
description: Strong coffee with brennivín and cream — the Icelandic answer to Irish coffee, with caraway in place of the sweetness.
funFact: Iceland drinks more coffee per head than almost anywhere on earth, and brennivín's caraway edge makes for a markedly drier coffee drink than the Irish version.

steps: Warm a glass mug and add the sugar.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the brennivín and stir once.
Float lightly whipped cream over the back of a spoon.
Drink through the cream without stirring.

name: Cà Phê Trứng Rum
description: Hanoi egg coffee with rum stirred through — egg yolk whipped with condensed milk into a meringue that sits on the coffee like a custard.
glassware: Small glass in a bowl of hot water
funFact: Egg coffee was invented in 1946 when a milk shortage in Hanoi led a Metropole bartender to whip egg yolk as a substitute; the café his family still runs serves it in glasses set in hot water.

steps: Brew strong Vietnamese coffee with a phin filter and keep it hot.
Whisk the egg yolk with the condensed milk until pale, thick and roughly tripled in volume.
Stir the rum into the hot coffee in a small glass.
Spoon the egg foam over the top so it floats as a distinct layer.
Stand the glass in a bowl of hot water and serve with a small spoon.

name: Nam Manao Soda
description: Thai rum with fresh lime soda and a pinch of salt — the format street vendors have sold for decades, given a measure of Sangsom.
funFact: The salt is not optional in Thai citrus drinks — it suppresses bitterness and lifts sweetness, which is why nam manao tastes rounder than a plain lime soda.

steps: Stir the lime juice, sugar syrup and salt together until the salt dissolves.
Fill a tall glass with ice and add the rum.
Pour in the lime mixture.
Top with cold soda water and stir once.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Palm Wine Punch
description: Fresh palm wine lengthened with citrus, ginger and a little gin — the village drink dressed for a Lagos party.
funFact: Palm wine ferments so fast that it changes character between morning and evening, which is why punches built on it are mixed to order rather than made ahead.

steps: Stir the ginger juice, lime juice and honey syrup together in a jug.
Add the gin and stir again.
Pour in the fresh palm wine last and stir gently once.
Serve over ice, immediately — it keeps fermenting in the glass.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Tej Spritz
description: Ethiopian honey wine lengthened with soda and citrus — the berele flask reimagined for a rooftop bar.
funFact: Gesho, the buckthorn that bitters tej, plays the same role hops play in beer — which is why tej takes to a spritz format better than most honey wines would.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the tej, lemon juice and honey syrup.
Top with soda water.
Stir once gently to combine.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Ceylon Arrack Sour
description: Coconut arrack shaken with lime, jaggery and egg white — the island's spirit given the sour treatment.
funFact: Jaggery — unrefined palm sugar — is the traditional sweetener here rather than cane sugar, and it gives the drink a smoky, caramel depth that simple syrup cannot.

steps: Dry-shake the arrack, lime juice, jaggery syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters over the foam.
Serve immediately.

name: Chacha Sour
description: Georgian grape marc spirit with lemon, honey and tarragon — the Caucasus answer to a pisco sour.
funFact: Tarragon is a defining Georgian flavour, most famously in the bright green tarkhuna soda, and it turns up in the country's modern bar scene as readily as mint does elsewhere.

steps: Press two tarragon sprigs gently in the shaker with the honey syrup.
Add the chacha, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a fresh tarragon sprig.

name: Moroccan Mint Cooler
description: Strong green tea with spearmint, sugar and a measure of fig brandy, served long over ice for the heat of the afternoon.
funFact: Moroccan mint tea is poured from a height to aerate it and build a foam head, a technique the cold version keeps purely because the tea tastes flat without it.

steps: Brew strong green tea with a generous handful of spearmint and cool it completely.
Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the fig brandy, sugar syrup and lemon juice.
Top with the cold mint tea, pouring from a height to aerate it.
Garnish with a large mint sprig.

name: Masala Chai Toddy
description: Spiced milk tea with dark rum stirred in — the roadside chai format given a winter measure.
funFact: Indian chai is boiled rather than steeped — tea, milk, sugar and spice all go into the pan together, which is why it tastes nothing like tea with milk added afterwards.

steps: Boil the water with the ginger, cardamom and sugar for two minutes.
Add the tea leaves and boil for another minute.
Pour in the milk and bring back to a boil, then simmer briefly.
Strain into a glass and stir in the rum off the heat.
Serve very hot.

name: Caju Amigo
description: Cachaça and cashew fruit juice — a two-ingredient northeastern staple made from the fruit the cashew nut hangs beneath.
funFact: The cashew nut grows on the outside of the cashew apple, a soft astringent fruit that is too perishable to export — which is why almost nobody outside Brazil has tasted its juice.

steps: Combine the cachaça and cashew juice in a small glass.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature, or over a single ice cube if the day is hot.
Drink in one or two mouthfuls, as a between-meal pick-me-up.

name: Vermut Torrontés
description: Argentine vermouth over ice with soda and an orange slice — the aperitivo hour that Italian immigrants brought and Argentina kept.
funFact: Argentina's vermouth tradition arrived with mass Italian immigration and nearly disappeared in the twentieth century; a wave of small Mendoza producers rebuilt it from the 2010s onward.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold vermouth.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and skewered olives.
Serve with something salty alongside.
